 When the calendar flips over to November, a large segment of the population understands that it’s Medicare Open Enrollment time again. It provides an opportunity for enrollees to review their coverage and consider switching their Medicare Advantage or Part D prescription plans.
 Those of us over 60 are likely to be inundated with letters, phone calls, text messages and e-mails offering new enrollment options. Unfortunately, some of those contacts will be from scammers. You can help protect yourself from these criminals if you understand what they’re after and some of the techniques they’re known to use.
 A common goal of criminals is to trick victims into giving up their Medicare number and other health information. Ploys used by criminals to get victims to disclose their personal data include:
 Calls offering free medical services or products.
 A caller offers to send you a new plastic Medicare card or a card with an electronic chip in it. Be aware that Medicare doesn’t issue plastic cards or ones with chips. All they provide is the paper version.
 E-mails that appear to be from Medicare informing you that your benefits are about to be blocked. This tactic hopes to frighten you into logging into a fake Medicare website so your credentials can be stolen.
 A caller, text, e-mail or letter that asks you to “confirm” or “verify” your Medicare number.
 A caller that pressures you to switch to a new plan.
 E-mails that contain a link that claims to lead to the Medicare website. Never click on a link in an e-mail. Open your Internet browser and enter the address Medicare.gov yourself.
 Scammers may offer free tests that will uncover or predict cancer, heart disease, Parkinsons, dementia, or other health concerns. These offers may be made via online ads, social media sites or via a telephone call. The scammer’s goal is to bill Medicare for these unprescribed tests. If Medicare denies payment for the claims, you might have to pay yourself.
 Threats that your coverage is about to be canceled unless you validate personal information such as your Medicare or Social Security numbers.
 Promises that you’re entitled to a refund related to Medicare coverage.
 All of the ploys listed above are merely ways to obtain your Medicare number or other personal information. Don’t be fooled. If someone you don’t recognize asks for your personal information, hang up or ignore the text or e-mail. No good will come from continuing contact with them.
 Ways criminals info
 Some ways that criminals abuse or make money from your Medicare number include:
 Phantom billing is submitting charges to Medicare for tests, doctor visits or medical equipment that a patient never received.
 Claims submitted under your name to pay for services, prescription drugs or medical supplies actually received by another person.
 Billing Medicare for tests, drugs, or medical equipment that you received, but didn’t actually need.
 Downsides for victims
 Victims may be billed for coinsurance costs for health services or drugs they didn’t receive.
 Victims may incorrectly reach coverage limits for inpatient hospital stays, thus limiting treatment they can obtain going forward.
 Claims made by criminals can become part of the victim’s health records. This can make it more difficult for their healthcare providers to have an accurate picture of the victim’s true health condition.
 Victims can spend a significant amount of time contacting insurers, Medicare and healthcare providers to remove false charges.
 Downside for Medicare
 Fraudulent claims hurt the entire Medicare system. Money lost to scammers isn’t being used for legitimate medical care for those the system should be helping. The exact amount of Medicare fraud that occurs annually is unknown. Two recent Federal enforcement actions exposed over $14.6 billion in one incident and $3.4 billion in another.
 Steps to take
 Scammers are always trying to victimize additional Medicare recipients, but there are steps you can take to protect yourself. These steps include:
 Don’t share your Medicare number or Social Security number with someone unless there is a legitimate need, for example, healthcare professionals in your doctor’s office. Never share details with an unknown person who called, e-mailed or texted you.
 It’s extremely unlikely that someone from Medicare will ever call you on the phone. This would only happen if they were returning a call or following up on something you requested. If you receive an unexpected call from someone claiming to be from Medicare there is a good chance it’s a scam. If you get a call like this, hang up and call Medicare directly using the number on the back of your Medicare card.
 Be extremely suspicious of Medicare-related ads, especially ads for free benefits on social media platforms. Watchdog groups say that Medicare-related scam ads on these platforms have increased significantly in recent years.
 Be extremely skeptical of callers who try to persuade you to switch to a different plan. If they claim the plan they’re pushing is “preferred by Medicare” they’re lying because Medicare doesn’t endorse any specific plans. If they threaten that your coverage will be shut down unless you switch plans, then it’s definitely a scam.
 Don’t allow any tests unless they are ordered by your doctor. Scammers send out test kits hoping that recipients will complete and return them. If you do, then Medicare will incur unnecessary billings and you may be responsible for copays.
 Never mail or send your Medicare card to anyone. One common scam is to tell victims that their card needs to be replaced. Turning your card over to an unknown caller will almost certainly cause problems.
 If you have become a victim of a Medicare scam or even suspect it, you should report it immediately. You can call Medicare directly at 1-800-633-4227. You can also call the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General at 1-800-447-8477.
 Kelly Bourne is the author of “Ransomware, Viruses, Social Engineering and Other Threats: Protecting Your Digital Assets.” He lives in Omaha, NE, and may be reached at kcbourne@cox.net .
